paragraphs: Distributed training combines updates from multiple workers, creating an opportunity for malicious participants to influence learning. Many defenses look for updates that sit far from the group average. This paper examines a different threat: coordinated changes small enough to blend into the natural variation among honest workers, without requiring knowledge of everyone else's data.

The attack depends on worker gradients having sufficiently high empirical variance. The authors find that this condition holds even on MNIST. In their demonstrations, malicious updates evade existing defenses and can exploit their selection rules, causing those defenses to favor malicious workers while rejecting legitimate contributions.

With fewer than 25% of workers colluding, the authors report a 50% degradation in model accuracy on MNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100. They also demonstrate backdoors that preserve ordinary accuracy on MNIST and CIFAR10, although accuracy declines on CIFAR100. These findings expose a weakness in defenses that associate malicious behavior primarily with conspicuously large deviations.
neurips-2019-a-little-is-enough-circumve.tldr: Small coordinated worker updates can exploit natural gradient variation to bypass distributed-learning defenses and damage or backdoor trained models.

paragraphs: A test set can influence model development when researchers repeatedly consult its scores. Over time, apparent improvements might reflect adaptation to that particular set rather than better performance on fresh data. This paper investigates how much evidence of that problem appears across more than one hundred Kaggle competitions spanning several years.

The competitions provide a useful comparison between two evaluation arrangements. Participants repeatedly receive feedback from a holdout set through a public leaderboard, while a separate test set is used only once to determine the final ranking. The authors systematically compare the public and final rankings to assess adaptation associated with repeated holdout use.

The analysis finds little evidence of substantial overfitting in these competitions. Its breadth makes that observation relevant across different data domains, loss functions, model classes, and practitioners. The result supports the practical robustness of holdout evaluation in the studied settings, while retaining an empirical scope: it does not establish that repeated test-set consultation can never cause overfitting.
neurips-2019-a-meta-analysis-of-overfitt.tldr: Across more than one hundred Kaggle competitions, comparisons of public and final rankings reveal little evidence of substantial overfitting from holdout reuse.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial networks and autoencoders offer different routes to learning generative models. Autoencoders also provide an encoder for reducing data to a feature representation, motivating efforts to combine their benefits with GAN performance. This paper asks whether f-GANs and Wasserstein autoencoders have a deeper mathematical connection behind their apparently different training objectives.

The authors establish a primal-dual relationship between those objectives: they can be understood as linked optimization formulations. Under specified assumptions, the objectives are equivalent. This conditional equivalence helps explain the success of Wasserstein autoencoders and supplies a route to proving generalization bounds for autoencoder models.

The analysis also connects the Wasserstein autoencoder objective to f-divergences and shows that it is upper bounded by the Wasserstein distance. That relationship opens a way to use existing regularized optimal transport solvers. Together, the results connect model design, generalization analysis, and optimization tools, taking a step toward a unified account of GANs and autoencoders without claiming unconditional equivalence between every version.
neurips-2019-a-primal-dual-link-between-.tldr: A conditional primal-dual equivalence connects f-GANs and Wasserstein autoencoders, enabling generalization bounds and links to optimal transport solvers.

paragraphs: Abstract reasoning requires identifying a pattern while ignoring features that happen to accompany it. This paper argues that distracting features are a major obstacle for deep learning systems on such tasks. Learning the relevant rule requires using counterexamples to reject plausible but incorrect hypotheses, rather than simply accumulating evidence for an initially attractive pattern.

The authors show that carefully arranging the progression through different training-data categories can reduce the effects of these distractions. They build on this observation with feature robust abstract reasoning, or FRAR. Its teacher network uses reinforcement learning to determine the training sequence, while a student network learns to make predictions.

The experiments report strong improvements over baseline algorithms, including improvements of 18.7% on RAVEN and 13.3% on PGM over the state-of-the-art models considered. These results support training order as a useful part of reasoning-system design. The contribution connects a specific learning obstacle—misleading features—to a mechanism for choosing the examples through which the student learns.
neurips-2019-abstract-reasoning-with-dis.tldr: FRAR uses a reinforcement-learning teacher to arrange training examples so a student can better learn abstract patterns despite distracting features.

paragraphs: Voice assistants rely on recognizing a wake word before responding to commands. This paper studies whether inconspicuous background music can interfere with that recognition and make an assistant unresponsive while the music is present. The target is the wake-word detector, so the intended effect is suppression of activation.

The researchers construct an emulated Alexa wake-word detector from published work and compare its detection accuracy with the real device. They generate adversarial audio using a differentiable synthesizer and account for transformations through an expectation-over-transform approach. Digital evaluation uses hundreds of utterance samples collected from the real world.

In those digital experiments, the emulated detector's F1 score falls from 93.4% to 11.0%. Playback over the air also affects Alexa, reducing its measured F1 score from 92.5% to 11.0%. The physical test is central to the finding: it demonstrates that the interference can survive playback and recording, rather than appearing only when audio is supplied digitally to an emulated model.
neurips-2019-adversarial-music-real-worl.tldr: Adversarial background music substantially reduced wake-word detection F1 in both an emulated detector and over-the-air tests against Alexa.

paragraphs: In conventional image recognition, viewing an image at a different scale should preserve its class. This paper uses that symmetry to generalize convolutional neural networks. Its aim is to make scale changes part of the network's mathematical structure, so internal computations respond to changes in viewing scale in a controlled way.

The proposed building blocks are scale-equivariant cross-correlations, developed as an extension of convolution using scale-space and semigroup theory. Equivariance means that changing the input scale produces a corresponding structured change in the representation. This relates the behavior of internal features across scales to the broader goal of recognizing the same class at different sizes.

Because cross-correlation is a basic network operation, the authors describe these components as suitable for plug-and-play use in almost any modern deep learning architecture. They demonstrate the networks on Patch Camelyon and Cityscapes and conduct introspective studies of their properties. The contribution is both an architectural operation and a principled account of how scale symmetry can shape image processing.
neurips-2019-deep-scale-spaces-equivaria.tldr: Deep scale-spaces extend convolution with scale-equivariant operations that can be incorporated into modern image-processing networks.

paragraphs: An anonymized histogram keeps the counts from a collection of label-count pairs while removing the labels themselves. The resulting object describes how frequently things occur without identifying which count belongs to which label. Such summaries arise in sensitive applications including password frequencies and the distribution of connection counts in social networks.

The paper proposes a differentially private mechanism for releasing these histograms. Its main theoretical result is a near-optimal trade-off between privacy and usefulness with respect to both the number of items and the privacy parameter. This addresses the accuracy of the released count information alongside the privacy requirement, rather than treating removal of labels as the entire solution.

The method also has a computational advantage when the input histogram is already represented compactly: its running time is sublinear in the number of items. For histograms sampled from an unknown discrete distribution, the released output can directly support estimation of symmetric properties. These are properties of the distribution that do not depend on how its labels are named.
neurips-2019-differentially-private-anon.tldr: The paper gives a differentially private anonymized-histogram mechanism with near-optimal utility and sublinear runtime when the input is compact.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether a voice recording can guide the generation of a face with characteristics associated with its speaker. The intended setting involves a previously unseen person. The task seeks shared identity-related elements between the generated face and the speaker, making the quality of that association central to the research question.

The proposed framework uses a generative adversarial network to produce faces from voices. During training, it learns by matching the identities of generated faces to those of the speakers. This gives the system a training signal linking the two kinds of information: an audio recording and a visual representation of a person.

Evaluation uses the related task of cross-modal matching to assess whether the generated faces correspond to their speakers. The authors report matching accuracy substantially above chance and agreement on several biometric characteristics. These findings support the presence of useful associations between voice and facial characteristics in the model's outputs; they do not amount to a claim that speech uniquely specifies an unseen person's exact face.
neurips-2019-face-reconstruction-from-vo.tldr: A GAN generates faces from voices that share several speaker characteristics and achieve cross-modal matching accuracy substantially above chance.

paragraphs: A neural network can reproduce sensory neurons' responses without making the underlying computation easy to understand. This paper addresses that gap between predicting a biological system's outputs and explaining how those outputs arise. It develops a systematic way to extract computational mechanisms from deep network models used in neuroscience.

The approach combines dimensionality reduction with attribution methods that assess the relative importance of interneurons for particular visual computations. Applied to retinal models, it yields an interpretation of the retina as a predictive feature extractor. In this account, responses signal departures from expectations across a variety of stimuli that change over space and time.

For each stimulus examined, the extracted mechanisms agree with prior scientific literature, and one case produces a new mechanistic hypothesis. Agreement provides support for the interpretation, while the new hypothesis offers a direction for experimental investigation. The broader contribution is a route from a successful predictive network to specific explanations of its computations, extending analysis beyond comparisons of neural representations alone.
neurips-2019-from-deep-learning-to-mecha.tldr: Dimensionality reduction and attribution reveal interpretable predictive mechanisms in retinal networks, including one new mechanistic hypothesis.

paragraphs: Comparing probability distributions is useful in generative modeling and other learning problems. Sliced-Wasserstein distance is attractive because it retains properties similar to Wasserstein distance while being much easier to compute. This paper studies the mathematical structure behind that comparison and uses it to construct a broader family of distribution distances.

The authors first clarify how sliced-Wasserstein distance connects to the Radon transform. They then use the generalized Radon transform to define generalized sliced-Wasserstein, or GSW, distances. They also develop a maximum version, called max-GSW, extending a corresponding idea available for the original sliced-Wasserstein construction.

An essential part of the work identifies conditions under which GSW and max-GSW are proper metrics. Those conditions establish when the proposed comparisons have the mathematical properties required of a distance, rather than assuming every construction qualifies. Numerical experiments on the generative modeling task of sliced-Wasserstein flows produce favorable results. The paper thus combines a generalization of an existing computational tool with theoretical checks and a focused empirical demonstration.
neurips-2019-generalized-sliced-wasserst.tldr: Generalized Radon transforms yield new sliced-Wasserstein distances, with conditions establishing metric validity and favorable results on generative flows.

paragraphs: Learning from observations asks an agent to imitate an expert using demonstrated states without access to the expert's actions. This could make resources such as videos useful for imitation, but removes part of the guidance available in learning from state-action demonstrations. The paper investigates what that missing information means theoretically and how to reduce its practical impact.

Within the modeling approach of generative adversarial imitation learning, the authors show that the gap between the two settings lies in disagreement between the expert's and imitator's inverse dynamics models. These models concern the actions associated with state changes. The result gives a specific mathematical account of what state-only imitation fails to constrain.

The authors identify negative causal entropy as an upper bound on this gap that can be minimized without a dynamics model. Their resulting method, Inverse-Dynamics-Disagreement-Minimization, augments conventional learning from observations with this objective. Experiments on challenging benchmarks show consistent improvements over other observation-only methods, supporting the usefulness of narrowing the theoretically identified gap.
neurips-2019-imitation-learning-from-obs.tldr: IDDM improves state-only imitation by minimizing an entropy-based bound on inverse-dynamics disagreement within a GAIL-based formulation.

paragraphs: Learning to optimize treats an optimization procedure itself as something that can be trained. This paper expands that idea beyond methods organized around individual search points and without explicit uncertainty awareness. Its meta-optimizer learns within an algorithmic space that includes both point-based and population-based approaches, allowing a group of candidate solutions to inform the search.

The update rule is represented through a population of LSTM networks equipped with attention across samples and features. Training uses a meta-loss containing cumulative regret and entropy. The method also estimates a posterior distribution directly over the global optimum and uses an uncertainty measure to guide learning, making uncertainty part of the optimization process.

Experiments on non-convex test functions and a protein-docking application show the proposed meta-optimizer outperforming the competitors considered. These findings support combining learned update rules, population information, and uncertainty estimates in the evaluated tasks. The contribution is an expanded framework for learning how to search, with attention and posterior estimation supplying information beyond a single candidate's position.
neurips-2019-learning-to-optimize-in-swa.tldr: A learned swarm optimizer combines attention-equipped LSTMs with uncertainty over the global optimum and outperforms tested competitors.

paragraphs: The paper studies linear regression when only a small subset of the model's coefficients are nonzero and some observed labels may be adversarially corrupted. The target is a vector with p coordinates and s nonzero entries, estimated from n samples. This combines the challenge of finding a sparse model with resistance to deliberately misleading outcomes.

The estimator combines an l1 penalty with Huber's estimation criterion. Under a Gaussian design and at most o corrupted labels, the authors prove an optimal convergence rate of sqrt(s/n) + o/n, up to a logarithmic factor. The expression separates the contribution associated with sparse estimation from the contribution associated with the fraction of contaminated labels.

The analysis also considers more general design matrices. It identifies the transfer principle and an incoherence property as sufficient for optimal robust-estimation rates when their constants are suitable. This extends the theoretical message beyond the Gaussian setting through explicit structural conditions. The result explains when this estimator can achieve optimal accuracy despite adversarial label contamination.
neurips-2019-outlier-robust-estimation-o.tldr: Under Gaussian design, l1-penalized Huber estimation achieves optimal sparse-regression rates up to logarithmic factors despite adversarial label outliers.

paragraphs: An unusual data point may stand out because of only a few of its attributes. PIDForest builds anomaly detection around this intuition: a small amount of information can distinguish an anomaly from the overwhelming majority of a dataset. The paper calls this principle partial identification and turns it into a geometric definition of unusualness.

Its measure, PIDScore, looks at subcubes containing a point and takes the minimum density of data points across them. In plain terms, the score asks whether the point belongs to a particularly sparsely occupied region defined through attribute ranges. The authors then introduce a random-forest-based algorithm that detects anomalies using this definition.

Across a broad range of benchmarks, PIDForest compares favorably with several popular anomaly-detection methods. It also supplies a compact explanation for each anomaly by identifying features and ranges that occur relatively rarely in the dataset. This makes the reason for a detection concrete: the method can point to an uncommon combination of attribute values as well as flagging the observation.
neurips-2019-pidforest-anomaly-detection.tldr: PIDForest detects anomalies through sparse attribute-defined regions and explains detections using uncommon feature ranges.

paragraphs: A spatial point process describes events distributed across space. Its intensity function predicts how many events occur in different locations, making intensity estimation central to spatial prediction. This paper develops a method that produces predictive intensity intervals, expressing predictions through ranges rather than relying only on a single estimated intensity.

The method learns a spatial model using a regularized criterion. Its central theoretical contribution is a guarantee about prediction performance outside the data used for fitting. Crucially, the guarantee remains valid when the spatial model is misspecified, meaning that the chosen model does not correctly describe the actual process generating the observations.

That robustness to misspecification matters because the prediction guarantee does not depend on having selected the correct spatial model. The authors contrast this property with standard estimators and demonstrate the method on both synthetic and real spatial data. The contribution brings interval prediction and theoretical out-of-sample assurance into the same modeling procedure, with model mismatch explicitly covered by the stated result.
neurips-2019-prediction-of-spatial-point.tldr: A regularized spatial model produces predictive intensity intervals with out-of-sample guarantees that remain valid under model misspecification.

paragraphs: This paper studies repeated selling to a buyer who follows a no-regret, mean-based learning algorithm. Earlier mechanisms could extract almost all economic surplus when buyer values were independent draws from a fixed distribution. The authors remove that distributional assumption, allowing values to be chosen adversarially and potentially adaptively across rounds.

Even in this prior-free setting, a mechanism can obtain a 1 − epsilon approximation to the full surplus for any positive epsilon. Its number of options per round is independent of the total number of rounds and has polynomial dependence on the approximation parameter. A lower bound requires at least order 1/epsilon options for that approximation, even with stochastic values, making the option complexity optimal up to a polynomial factor.

The authors also examine a constrained auction format where overbidding is dominated. Here they obtain the previously established approximation order when the value distribution is unknown, and an order 1/log H approximation under adversarial values. These results distinguish what general mechanisms can extract from what is achievable under the additional auction-format restriction.
neurips-2019-prior-free-dynamic-auctions.tldr: Repeated-sale mechanisms can extract nearly all surplus from a no-regret, mean-based buyer even with adversarial values, with weaker results under auction-format restrictions.

paragraphs: Point-cloud registration aligns two collections of spatial points describing a shape. When both collections show only part of the shape, the system must work out which visible points correspond while also determining the alignment. PRNet addresses this partial-to-partial setting, extending beyond earlier learning-based methods that assume the entire shape is visible.

The network jointly learns three connected components: a geometric representation, a detector for keypoints shared between partial views, and correspondences between those keypoints. It uses self-supervision to learn these components together. Deep networks tackle the non-convex alignment and partial-correspondence problem, linking the choice of useful points to the task of matching them.

On synthetic data, PRNet outperforms PointNetLK, DCP, and the non-learning methods considered. The authors also show consistent keypoint and correspondence predictions across views and objects. Beyond registration, the learned representation transfers to classification. These results suggest that learning to connect partial observations can produce both useful alignment information and geometric features applicable to another task.
neurips-2019-prnet-self-supervised-learn.tldr: PRNet jointly learns representations, shared keypoints, and correspondences to align partial point clouds through self-supervision.

paragraphs: High-dimensional Bayesian inference must represent uncertainty over a large collection of parameters. This paper proposes projected Stein variational Newton, or pSVN, to exploit situations where the posterior distribution has an intrinsic geometric structure of much lower dimension. The method uses that structure to concentrate its sample updates in a smaller subspace.

The subspace is constructed from curvature information supplied by the Hessian of the log posterior. At the current samples, the method averages Hessian information and uses its eigenvectors to identify the projection directions. It then updates the projected parameter samples in parallel using Stein variational Newton. Because the subspace is adaptive, its construction responds to the current samples.

The authors demonstrate fast convergence, complexity independent of parameter and sample dimensions, and parallel scalability. The underlying approach connects these computational properties to exploiting low-dimensional posterior geometry within a much larger parameter space. Its main contribution is an inference procedure that combines adaptive geometric projection with parallel sample updates, rather than carrying out every update in the full parameter space.
neurips-2019-projected-stein-variational.tldr: pSVN uses adaptive Hessian-based projections and parallel sample updates to exploit low-dimensional structure in high-dimensional Bayesian inference.

paragraphs: Extracellular recordings capture electrical activity through electrodes outside neurons. Determining where individual spikes originate helps researchers investigate the functional organization of neural circuits. This paper develops a Bayesian model for localizing those spike sources using high-density microelectrode arrays, treating location as something to infer from the recorded signals.

To make inference scalable, the authors implement the model as a variational autoencoder and use amortized variational inference. The central idea of amortization is to share a learned inference procedure across observations, so source estimation can reuse that procedure for individual spikes. This connects the Bayesian localization model to a neural-network implementation designed for repeated inference.

Evaluation includes both biophysically realistic simulations and real extracellular recordings. The authors report more accurate localization than heuristic methods such as center of mass, along with the ability to improve spike sorting performance. That second finding connects location estimates to another practical recording-analysis task: better localization can also help the process of separating recorded spikes by their neuronal sources.
neurips-2019-scalable-spike-source-local.tldr: A Bayesian spike-localization model implemented as a variational autoencoder improves localization accuracy and can improve spike sorting over heuristic methods.

paragraphs: Models trained on separate datasets may contain related underlying structures even when the datasets differ. This paper studies how to aggregate such models when their training data remain sequestered. The task is to identify what their learned parameterizations have in common and use those correspondences to construct shared global structure.

The proposed framework uses Bayesian nonparametric tools to perform this matching. It operates as a meta-model over local model parameterizations, learning correspondences between them rather than starting from a pooled dataset. The authors describe the approach as model-independent and applicable to a wide range of model types, making parameter matching the common organizing principle.

After verification on simulated data, the paper demonstrates aggregation of Gaussian topic models, hierarchical Dirichlet process hidden Markov models, and sparse Gaussian processes. The associated applications include text summarization, motion-capture analysis, and temperature forecasting. This variety illustrates the framework's intended breadth: shared latent structure can be sought across independently learned models in several distinct statistical settings.
neurips-2019-statistical-model-aggregati.tldr: A Bayesian nonparametric framework aggregates separately trained models by matching their parameters to learn shared latent structure.

paragraphs: Traffic datasets often omit an explicit description of how sensors relate within a road network. Those that include such structure commonly focus on urban centers or highways and rely on costly sensors. STREETS addresses a different setting: suburban traffic observed through publicly available web cameras, paired with network information.

The dataset contains more than four million still images collected over 2.5 months from one hundred cameras in suburban Lake County, Illinois. The cameras are divided into two communities represented by directed graphs. Vehicle counts provide traffic statistics, connecting the image collection to measurements of traffic activity across the camera network.

The authors provide benchmark tasks and baseline results for one task to help researchers use the dataset. Their goal is to support investigation of inexpensive, non-invasive cameras for understanding traffic in communities of different sizes. The contribution is therefore both a large image resource and a structured suburban network setting in which researchers can study relationships among traffic observations.
neurips-2019-streets-a-novel-camera-netw.tldr: STREETS pairs over four million suburban traffic images with camera-network graphs and vehicle counts to support traffic-flow research.

paragraphs: This paper studies sampling from distributions proportional to exp(−f(x)), where f is strongly convex and has a Lipschitz-continuous gradient. These assumptions describe a structured class of log-concave distributions. The authors propose a Markov chain Monte Carlo method based on underdamped Langevin diffusion, a continuous stochastic process that converges to the desired distribution.

The contribution is a new framework for turning differential equations into discrete simulation steps. Applied to Langevin diffusion, it reaches error epsilon times D in 2-Wasserstein distance in roughly kappa^(7/6)/epsilon^(1/3) + kappa/epsilon^(2/3) steps, suppressing logarithmic factors. Here kappa measures conditioning and D = sqrt(d/m) sets the problem's effective scale.

This improves the stated previous step bound of roughly kappa^(3/2)/epsilon. The algorithm can also be parallelized to require O(kappa log(1/epsilon)) parallel steps. These are theoretical efficiency results under the stated smoothness and convexity assumptions. Beyond sampling, the authors present the discretization framework as applicable to other problems involving simulation of ordinary or stochastic differential equations.
neurips-2019-the-randomized-midpoint-met.tldr: A new Langevin discretization improves theoretical sampling complexity for smooth, strongly log-concave distributions and supports efficient parallelization.

paragraphs: Medical imaging models often start from large architectures and weights pretrained on natural images such as ImageNet. This paper investigates what that transfer actually contributes, given differences in dataset sizes, visual features, and task requirements. It separates the question of final performance from the question of which learned features are being reused.

On two large-scale medical imaging tasks, the authors find that transfer provides little performance benefit and that simple, lightweight models can perform comparably to ImageNet architectures. Analysis of learned representations suggests that some differences associated with transfer arise from having more model parameters than needed, rather than from sophisticated reuse of pretrained features.

The study also identifies where useful feature reuse occurs and explores benefits from weight scaling that do not depend on transferred features. These distinctions matter for efficient model exploration: pretrained weights may affect learning through several mechanisms, and a large pretrained architecture is not automatically the source of better performance. The findings apply to the evaluated tasks and motivate closer examination of what transfer contributes in a particular setting.
neurips-2019-transfusion-understanding-t.tldr: On two large medical-imaging tasks, ImageNet transfer offers little performance benefit, and some effects arise from model size and weight scaling rather than feature reuse.

paragraphs: The discount factor affects how reinforcement-learning systems value future rewards, but it also changes the optimization problem. This paper designs experiments to isolate its different effects. The authors revisit the common explanation that low discount factors perform poorly because the differences between action values, called action gaps, become too small.

Their alternative hypothesis emphasizes how much action-gap sizes vary across states. If those differences have very different scales in different parts of the state space, learning can become difficult. The proposed method maps value estimates into logarithmic space to make action gaps more homogeneous, directly addressing this variation in scale.

The authors prove convergence under standard assumptions and empirically show that the method enables lower discount factors in approximate reinforcement learning. They report that this makes a class of problems accessible that traditional methods find challenging. The work therefore connects an experimental reassessment of a familiar optimization explanation to a concrete change in value representation, while treating the proposed cause as a hypothesis.
neurips-2019-using-a-logarithmic-mapping.tldr: Mapping value estimates into logarithmic space makes action gaps more homogeneous and empirically enables lower discount factors in approximate reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Label smoothing replaces a fully concentrated training target with a mixture of that target and a uniform distribution over classes. It discourages overconfident predictions and can improve learning speed and generalization. This paper investigates its effects more closely, asking how benefits to prediction relate to changes in the information learned by a network.

The authors empirically find improved calibration, meaning better agreement between prediction confidence and correctness, which can significantly improve beam search. They also observe a drawback for knowledge distillation: when the teacher is trained with label smoothing, transferring its knowledge to a student becomes much less effective.

Visualizations of the penultimate layer provide an explanation. Label smoothing encourages examples from the same class to form tight clusters, removing information from the logits about similarities between examples belonging to different classes. That information is needed for distillation, even though its loss does not hurt the model's generalization or calibration in the reported findings. The study explains why an effective predictive model can be a less effective teacher.
neurips-2019-when-does-label-smoothing-h.tldr: Label smoothing improves generalization and calibration but can weaken distillation by removing cross-class similarity information from a teacher's logits.
